legacyBodyWas: CRITICAL - Suspected cancer = ALWAYS apply Urgent Referral rules, even if the word "urgent" is absent.
canonicalBodyNow: Suspected cancer does not automatically define task type independently of the task/context; preserve urgency exactly as supported.

legacyBodyWas: CRITICAL - Smoking and drinking: ALWAYS include (positive or negative), EXCEPT when writing to an occupational therapist.
canonicalBodyNow: Smoking/alcohol are not universal always-include facts; relevance and reader needs control content.

legacyBodyWas: CRITICAL - Allergy: ALWAYS include (positive or negative) for atopic conditions (asthma, eczema, hay fever). For non-atopic conditions, include allergy only if relevant to the condition or its medication.
canonicalBodyNow: Allergy inclusion is relevance/safety driven; the atopic-condition rule is a heuristic, not an official absolute.

legacyBodyWas: Appositive clause: "Ms Miller, a 25-year-old teacher, presented with..." - use "gentleman" for males, "lady" for females (not man/woman). canonicalBodyNow: Gentleman/lady is unnecessary and may be dated; use patient/person or an appropriate identifier.

legacyBodyWas: CRITICAL - Next visit reference: "on the following visit" / "later on" / "later that month". NEVER "next visit".
canonicalBodyNow: Next visit is standard English; following visit may be stylistically preferable in some narratives but is not mandatory.

legacyBodyWas: CRITICAL - Resolved conditions and surgery -> PAST SIMPLE. "She had a cholecystectomy in 2018." Never use present perfect for surgery.
canonicalBodyNow: Present perfect is valid with procedures when current relevance/no finished time supports it (has undergone).

legacyBodyWas: Past perfect (had + past participle): AVOID in OET. Alternative: ING form or noun. "She reported non-compliance with the advice given."
canonicalBodyNow: Past perfect is valid when needed to establish earlier-past chronology; do not ban it.

legacyBodyWas: Reported speech - after reported/mentioned/stated/described: use ING or noun. "She reported having headaches." NOT "...that she had had headaches."
canonicalBodyNow: That-clauses are grammatically valid after report/state/mention; gerund/noun forms are alternatives, not the only forms.

legacyBodyWas: CRITICAL - Always include numerical values with units when given. Example: "glucose of 7.8 mmol/L." Never write the reference range.
canonicalBodyNow: Do not always include every numerical value; include values that are relevant to purpose/reader and preserve units accurately.

legacyBodyWas: Clinic scheduling fractions: 1/4 = once a week; 1/12 = once a year; 3/52 = three times a year; 3/7 = three times a week; 8/24 = eight-hourly; 12/24 = twice a day. canonicalBodyNow: Legacy fraction conversions are unsafe/incorrect as a universal rule; interpret source notation from context and never guess.

legacyBodyWas: CRITICAL - Never use the word "patient" in the body. Use last name + title, or a pronoun.
canonicalBodyNow: The word patient is not grammatically or officially forbidden; use names/pronouns/patient according to clarity and style.

legacyBodyWas: Replace "tired" with "fatigue." Replace "bad" with "poor" or "inadequate." No colloquial language.
canonicalBodyNow: Do not replace tired with fatigue automatically; they can differ in meaning and register.

legacyBodyWas: CRITICAL - "However": always preceded by semicolon; comma follows. Pattern: "[clause]; however, [clause]."
canonicalBodyNow: However can start a sentence or follow a semicolon; no single punctuation pattern is mandatory.

legacyBodyWas: "Therefore" / "Thus": preceded by semicolon; comma follows. Pattern: "[clause]; therefore, [clause]."
canonicalBodyNow: Therefore/thus have more than one correct punctuation pattern; apply standard punctuation by sentence structure.

legacyBodyWas: "In addition" (joining two complete clauses): semicolon before + comma after. "[Clause]; in addition, [clause]."
canonicalBodyNow: In addition can be sentence-initial or clause-linked; do not require a semicolon in every case.

legacyBodyWas: "As" (meaning because) in mid-sentence: comma before. "Treatment was changed, as the patient showed no improvement."
canonicalBodyNow: A comma before causal as is context-dependent, not universal.

legacyBodyWas: "For which": comma before. "She has hypertension, for which she was commenced on amlodipine."
canonicalBodyNow: Comma before for which depends on whether the relative clause is non-restrictive; not every occurrence needs one.

legacyBodyWas: Appositive: between two commas. "Ms Miller, a 25-year-old teacher, presented with..." Use "gentleman" / "lady" (not man/woman).
canonicalBodyNow: Gentleman/lady is not required; use neutral professional identifiers.

legacyBodyWas: CRITICAL - Any ongoing medical condition with active medications MUST be mentioned, even if unrelated to the urgent issue.
canonicalBodyNow: Do not include every active condition/medicine automatically; relevance and continuity/safety govern inclusion.

legacyBodyWas: CRITICAL - Do NOT include: family history, social history, smoking/drinking, previous medical history, occupation. GP knows all of this.
canonicalBodyNow: Social/family/past history can be relevant to discharge if it changed or affects ongoing care; do not exclude categorically.

legacyBodyWas: CRITICAL - All investigations performed during admission (including normal results) MUST be listed with values.
canonicalBodyNow: Do not list all investigations including all normal results; select what the reader needs.

legacyBodyWas: Past tense throughout (all events occurred during admission).
canonicalBodyNow: Discharge letters use tense according to time: past for admission events, present for current status, future/modal for plan.

legacyBodyWas: CRITICAL - Do NOT use medical jargon. Translate: "hypertension" -> "high blood pressure"; avoid abbreviations like "BP" unless previously spelled out.
canonicalBodyNow: Technicality should match the recipient. Allied-health professionals may understand clinical terminology; explain/simplify for the actual reader.

legacyBodyWas: CRITICAL - Most heavily weighted for pass/fail: Content and Conciseness & Clarity.
canonicalBodyNow: OET does not publish a simple pass/fail weighting formula that makes two criteria universally decisive.

legacyBodyWas: Required score: approximately Band 6+ in most criteria; at least Band 2 out of 3 in Purpose.
canonicalBodyNow: Do not convert descriptors into a universal regulator pass threshold; regulator requirements vary.

legacyBodyWas: CRITICAL - Examiner standard: "Could this letter be sent in a real clinical setting?" Yes = pass. No = fail.
canonicalBodyNow: Could this be sent clinically is a useful heuristic, not the official pass/fail formula.
